analysis.one_liner: Repeals the law requiring union-scale prevailing wages on federally funded construction projects.
analysis.headline: Backed by 24 Republican senators and reported out of committee in May 1995, the Davis-Bacon repeal never received a Senate floor vote and died when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill, sponsored by Sen. Nancy Kassebaum with 23 Republican cosponsors, would repeal the Davis-Bacon Act, which requires contractors on federally funded construction to pay the locally prevailing wage, and the Copeland Act, which requires contractor payroll reports designed to prevent kickbacks from workers' pay [S2]. A committee amendment would also strike prevailing-wage requirements from Tennessee Valley Authority contracts [S3]. The Senate Labor Committee reported it favorably in May 1995 and placed it on the Senate calendar, but it never came to a vote before the Congress ended [S6].
analysis.who_benefits: Federal construction contractors — especially smaller and nonunion firms — could win more federal work by paying below the locally prevailing wage, and all federal contractors would be freed from Copeland Act payroll reporting [S2, S4]. Taxpayers could see lower bids on federal construction, though the savings depend on contractors actually passing lower labor costs through [S4].

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Davis-Bacon Act, which requires the locally prevailing wage for laborers and mechanics on federally financed or federally assisted construction, allowing contractors to pay lower rates on those jobs
Repeals Section 2 of the Copeland Act, ending the payroll reporting requirement from federal contractors that was designed to prevent kickbacks, reducing paperwork and recordkeeping
Strikes provisions of the Tennessee Valley Authority Act requiring TVA contractors to pay prevailing wage rates, added by committee amendment
States its purposes as creating job opportunities, saving costs on federal construction contracts, promoting small-business participation in federal contracting, and reducing paperwork

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers on federally financed projects, who would no longer be guaranteed the locally prevailing wage and could see their pay drop [S2]. Unionized contractors and building-trades workers would also face competition from lower-wage bids on federal jobs [S2].

drawbacks.text: Construction workers on federal projects would lose the guarantee of the locally prevailing wage, removing the federal wage floor for those jobs and likely cutting pay where prevailing rates exceed what nonunion contractors pay
Repealing the Copeland Act eliminates the payroll reports that exist to prevent kickbacks from workers' pay and to verify wages were actually paid, removing a layer of oversight
The promised taxpayer savings assume contractors pass lower wage costs through in their bids; if bids don't fall in step, workers absorb the pay cut and the public doesn't see the savings

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real but modest gains — lower labor costs and less reporting paperwork for federal contractors, with potentially lower bids for taxpayers. Against that, its direct effect is a pay cut for a defined group of construction workers and the removal of payroll records used to catch kickbacks and wage violations. Because the savings depend on competitive bidding behavior the bill cannot guarantee, the costs fall with more certainty than the benefits arrive. The outcome was never tested: the bill never reached a floor vote.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Labor Committee reported the bill favorably and placed it on the Senate calendar in May 1995, but no vote was ever scheduled and it died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Sen. Nancy Kassebaum introduced the bill on January 4, 1995, joined by 23 Republican cosponsors, and it was referred to the Labor and Human Resources Committee
The committee held hearings on February 15, 1995 (printed as S.Hrg. 104-18) and ordered the bill reported favorably with amendments on March 29, 1995
On May 12, 1995, Kassebaum reported the bill with amendments (Report 104-80) and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 105
After a star print was ordered on the Senate report in June 1996, no further action was taken; the bill sat on the calendar until the Congress ended on January 3, 1997, without a floor vote

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal construction workers and the union building trades, who kept the prevailing-wage floor and Copeland payroll-reporting protections because the repeal never passed. Contractors who would have gained the ability to pay below prevailing wage got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Construction workers who kept wage protections

sides.party_line_note: All 24 senators who sponsored or cosponsored the bill were Republicans and no Democrat signed on; the bill never reached a floor vote, so no roll call shows where the parties stood.

industries.note: Davis-Bacon prevailing-wage rules underpin union-scale pay on federal construction; repeal would let nonunion bids pay below those rates and undercut union contractors. Their loss would be a wage loss for their workers.

Repeal opens federal work to firms paying below the local prevailing wage, and the bill explicitly aims to promote small-business participation. Their gain comes out of construction workers' pay on federal projects.

All federal contractors would be relieved of Copeland Act payroll reporting, a genuine administrative saving, but the requirement being lifted is the one designed to prevent kickbacks from workers' pay and to document that wages were paid.
